transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor... I, uh, I guess my wife really pushed me to come in, mostly. Because I’m just... I’m stuck on this thing, this issue with my face. I work construction, right? Have since I was right out of high school, so I know I’m no model. I know I've got some miles on me and I'm out in the sun a lot. But there’s this... this patch on the side of my face. It’s not just normal aging, it’s this rough, completely sunken-looking area. Like the skin just collapsed or gave out or something. 

I just can’t stop looking at it. Every morning I’m in the bathroom mirror for I don't even know how long, just turning my head, staring at how beat-up and old that one specific side of me looks. I check it in the rearview mirror of my truck when I'm parked at the site, too. And if someone takes a photo? Forget about it, it’s all I can see. We had a family barbecue a couple weeks ago and I completely ruined the whole mood because I saw a picture my daughter took and that rough, sunken patch just jumped right out at me. I couldn't even look at the rest of the picture. 

But the crazy part—and why I’m sitting in this chair, I guess—is that people keep telling me I'm making a big deal out of nothing. My wife, the guys on the crew, they all swear they barely notice anything at all. They say it's just a shadow or just normal skin, but... I mean, I have eyes, Doc. I see it every single day. I don't know how they can stand there and tell me they don't see how messed up it is.
Is this patch on your face the only thing that bothers you about your appearance?

Well, yeah, pretty much. I mean, look at me, Doc. I’m a fifty-two-year-old guy who’s been hauling lumber and pouring concrete since the late eighties. I know I’m not winning any beauty pageants, and I honestly don't care to. I’ve got, uh, I've got scars all over my hands, my knuckles are permanently swollen, I've got a nasty scar right here under my chin from where a piece of rebar caught me back in '98... and none of that bothers me. Not one bit. 

I don't care that my hair's thinning out or that I've got a bit of a gut on me now. That’s just... that's just life, right? That’s what happens when you work hard and get older. You get some wear and tear. I'm completely fine with all of that. My wife loves me, I provide for my family, I don't need to look perfect. 

But this patch... it’s different. It’s not a badge of honor like a work scar. It just looks wrong. Like the skin is just decaying or collapsing in on itself. So, no, I’m not one of those guys who spends hours worrying about his muscles or his nose or whatever else. It’s literally just this one specific area. If I could just fix this one sunken spot, or get it smoothed out somehow, I wouldn't give a second thought to anything else in the mirror. I’d be perfectly happy just being a regular, rough-around-the-edges guy. But because of this one spot... I just, I can't look past it. It just ruins the whole picture.
Has this concern about the patch on your face affected your work or relationships in any way?

Well, I mean... yeah, it has. It really has, and that's the part that really gets to me, you know? Because I’ve always been the guy who shows up early. For thirty years, I’m the first truck in the lot, drinking my coffee, waiting for the foreman to unlock the gate. But lately... lately, I’ve been late getting out the door. More than a few times. Because I get stuck in the bathroom just staring at it, trying to see if the lighting makes it look worse today, or if I can somehow hold my head at an angle where that sunken part doesn't look so obvious. My wife will be calling up the stairs that my lunch is packed and I’m just... I can't pull myself away. 

And at work, we have to take these site photos, right? Progress shots for the client or the contractor. I used to just jump in them, throw a thumbs up, whatever. Now? I’m dodging them like the plague. If I see the super pull out his phone to snap a picture of the crew, I suddenly have to go check a measurement on the other side of the site, or I pretend I need to grab something from the truck. I just can't stand the thought of that patch being captured on camera again, especially where other people might look at it later. 

And it’s not just work, either. It’s bleeding into my home life, which is why my wife is so fed up. We used to do these family game nights, you know? My daughter and her husband come over, we order pizza, play cards. Nothing fancy, just sitting around the kitchen table. But the lighting right over our table... it casts this shadow straight down, and I know exactly how it hits that spot on my face. It makes it look ten times deeper, like a crater. So the last couple of times, I just... I skipped it. I told them I was too beat from work, or my back was acting up, and I just stayed in the bedroom watching TV in the dark. I just didn't want them sitting across from me, staring at my face under that light for two hours. It’s just... it’s exhausting, Doc, having to think about it all the time.
Do you ever think that maybe the patch on your face isn't as noticeable as you think it is?

Well, that's the thing, right? That's what my wife says, that's what the guys at the site say. They all tell me I'm crazy, that it's just a shadow, that they don't even see it. And sometimes, you know, when I'm driving home and the sun is setting behind me, and the cab of the truck is kind of dim, I'll catch a glimpse in the mirror and think, okay, maybe it's not so bad. Maybe they're right. Maybe I'm just getting older and my skin is changing and I'm just hyper-focused on this one spot. 

I mean, I try to tell myself that. I really do. I'll sit there at the red light on 4th and Main, right by the old hardware store, and I'll tell myself, 'Frank, you're a fifty-two-year-old construction worker, nobody expects you to look like George Clooney.' I try to rationalize it. I try to think about how lighting works, how shadows fall. I even bought this special magnifying mirror for the bathroom, thinking maybe if I look at it really close up, I'll see that it's just normal pores or something. But then... then I turn the bathroom light on. The bright, overhead one, the one that really shows everything. And boom, there it is. 

It's like all that rationalizing just goes right out the window. Because I see it. I see the way the skin dips down, the way it looks rough and collapsed. And I just can't unsee it. It's like, how can they not see this? Are they just being nice? Are they just trying to make me feel better because they know how much it bothers me? My wife, God bless her, she's the sweetest woman in the world, she wouldn't want to hurt my feelings. But sometimes I wonder if she's just saying it's not noticeable because she's tired of hearing me talk about it. Or maybe they really don't see it the way I do, but that doesn't change the fact that it's there. I know it's there. I feel it when I wash my face, I see it in the pictures... so, yeah, sometimes I try to convince myself it's not a big deal, but it never lasts. It always comes back to me staring at it and knowing how messed up it looks.
Do you think it's possible that the patch on your face is not as severe as you think it is, or that it's not there at all?

Not there at all? I mean... Doc, look, I know I just said that I try to talk myself down sometimes, but to say it's not there *at all*? No. No way. I wouldn't be sitting here in your office, missing a full day's pay, if it was just thin air. 

The whole reason I’m even here talking to a professional is because I literally can’t stop seeing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. It's in every mirror, it's in the photos... it just makes it look like one whole side of me is just incredibly old and beat-up, like the structure underneath is just giving out. And I know we just went over this, how my wife and the guys at the site keep saying they barely notice anything, or that it's just a trick of the light. But a camera doesn't have an imagination, you know? A camera lens just captures what's physically sitting in front of it. And when I see those progress shots at work, back before I started dodging them, it was right there. Rough, caved in, making me look lopsided. 

So, no, I can't buy that it's not there or that I'm just making it up. I wish I could. Believe me, I'd love nothing more than to wake up, turn on that bright bathroom light, and just see a normal, symmetrical fifty-two-year-old face looking back at me. But I don't. I see that patch, and I can't stop staring at it, and it just eats away at my whole day. I wouldn't be putting my wife through all this stress, or hiding in my bedroom in the dark instead of seeing my daughter, if it wasn't real. It's there, and I just don't know how to fix it.
Have you ever considered the possibility that the patch on your face might not be as physically noticeable to others as it is to you, but rather something that you alone perceive?

Something I alone perceive? Like... like it's a hallucination or something? I don't... I really don't know what you mean by that, Doc. I mean, I'm a construction worker. I deal with physical things all day long. If a foundation is cracked, it's cracked. You don't stand there with your hands in your pockets wondering if you're the only guy on the crew perceiving the crack, right? You get the tools and you patch it. That's just how my brain works. 

So when I look in the mirror—like, okay, take the mirror in our downstairs half-bath. We remodeled that room about five years ago, put in these frosted glass sconces on either side of the medicine cabinet. My wife picked them out at Home Depot because they're supposed to give off this soft, flattering light. But even in that light, when I'm standing there at the sink, washing the grease off my hands with that gritty orange pumice soap after a ten-hour shift... I look up, and I see it. It's a physical dip in the skin. The shadow literally catches right in the groove of it. 

I just renewed my commercial driver's license a while back, and I passed the vision test with flying colors. My eyes work perfectly fine. So if I'm standing two feet away from a mirror, staring right at my own face, and I can literally trace the outline of how rough and sunken it is... how could it just be me? I haven't really considered that it's something only I can see because... well, because I'm looking right at a physical thing. I just don't understand how a structural defect on my skin could only be visible to my eyes and nobody else's. It just doesn't make any sense to me. If it's there, it's there, you know?
Have you ever thought that maybe you're the only one who can see this patch on your face because it's not actually there physically?

Doc, I feel like we're just going around in circles here. I mean, didn't I just answer that? I'm here—I'm literally sitting in this chair right now, missing a whole day's pay—because I can’t stop seeing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. Every single time I look in a mirror, every time someone snaps a photo at a family barbecue or on the job site, it's right there. It makes it look like one whole side of me is just incredibly old and beat-up, like the skin is just completely giving up and collapsing. 

And yeah, I know I already told you that my wife and the guys at work keep saying they barely notice anything. They tell me it's nothing, or just a shadow. But I can't just turn off my own eyes, you know? Just yesterday, I spent probably forty-five minutes standing in the upstairs hallway. We have this mirror right by the linen closet, and around four o'clock, the afternoon sun comes through the window at this specific angle. I just stood there, tilting my head back and forth, just staring at how the skin dips down. My wife came upstairs with a basket of laundry and caught me doing it again, and I just... I felt so ridiculous, but I couldn't pull myself away. 

So, no, I haven't ever thought it's not actually physically there. If it wasn't there, I wouldn't be wasting my life staring at it. I wouldn't be avoiding cameras or spending half an hour just analyzing the texture of my own cheek in the hallway. I'm telling you, it's a physical thing, and it's ruining my life, regardless of whether anyone else wants to admit they see it.
Do you think it's possible that your brain is playing a trick on you and the patch on your face isn't actually there?

Doc... I really, really don't mean to be disrespectful here, but I feel like you're not listening to me. We've been over this like three times now. A trick? My brain is playing a trick on me? 

Look, I get it. You're a doctor. You deal with the mind, with people who see things that aren't there, people who hear voices, whatever. But I'm a fifty-two-year-old man who has worked in construction since I was eighteen. I don't have an overactive imagination. I deal with concrete, rebar, drywall. Things you can touch. Things you can measure. 

If I'm standing in my bathroom, right? The one with the frosted sconces my wife bought. I'm standing there, and I can literally feel the texture of my skin. I can see the dip, the way the light casts a shadow right into that sunken patch. It's not a mirage. It's not some magic trick my brain is pulling on me like one of those optical illusions you see on the internet, where a dress is blue or gold or whatever. This is my face. I've had this face for over half a century. I know what it's supposed to look like, and I know what it looks like now. 

And it's not just the bathroom mirror! It's the rearview mirror in my truck when I'm driving to the site at five in the morning. It's the reflection in the microwave door when I'm heating up my coffee. It's everywhere. If my brain is playing a trick on me, then it's a trick that's happening twenty-four hours a day, in every lighting condition, from every angle. And that just... that doesn't make sense. 

I'm telling you, I wouldn't be missing work, I wouldn't be avoiding my own daughter, I wouldn't be driving my wife crazy asking her to look at it if it was just a trick. It's real. It's physical. And I just need someone to help me figure out how to fix it, not tell me I'm imagining things. So, no, I don't think it's possible. I just don't.
Do you think it's possible that your concern about the patch on your face is worse than the actual appearance of it?

Doc, I... look, I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. We just keep coming back to the exact same thing, don't we? You're asking if my concern is worse than the actual appearance. But the appearance *is* the concern. That's the whole point. That's why I'm sitting here in this office on a Tuesday morning when I should be out on the site tying rebar for the new parking garage over on 4th Street. 

I mean, I've told you already, right? I'm here because I just can't stop seeing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. It's like... it's like my skin is just collapsing in on itself. And it's not just a passing thought. It's every time I look in the mirror. It's every time someone pulls out a phone to take a picture at a family barbecue, or even just a quick snapshot at the job site when the foreman wants to document our progress. I see the photo later, and my eyes just zero right in on it. It makes it look like one whole side of me is just incredibly old and beat-up. Like I've aged twenty years on just the left side of my face. 

And yeah, I know I've said this before, but it bears repeating because it seems like you're getting hung up on this idea that I'm overreacting. My wife, the guys at work... they keep saying they barely notice anything. They tell me it's just a shadow, or it's the lighting, or it's just how skin looks when you're fifty-two and you've worked outside your whole life. But how can I believe them when I see it so clearly? How can my concern be worse than the appearance when the appearance is exactly what's causing the concern? 

I just... I can't let it go. It's not like a bad haircut that's going to grow out in a couple of weeks, you know? It's my face. It's the first thing people see when they look at me. And when I see that sunken patch, it's all I can focus on. So, no, I don't think my concern is worse than the appearance. I think my concern is exactly as bad as the appearance, because the appearance is what's ruining my life right now. It's what's keeping me from living normally. I just don't understand how you're not getting that.
Have you ever considered seeking a second opinion from a dermatologist to confirm whether the patch on your face is physically present?

A dermatologist? I... well, no, I haven't really thought about doing that. I mean, I guess I just don't see the point in going to a skin doctor just to have them tell me what I already know is sitting right there on my face. You know? It's not like I have a rash or, or some weird mole that needs freezing off. 

We get guys on the job site all the time who have to go in to those kinds of doctors because they've been out in the sun for thirty years and they get those little spots, you know, the ones they have to scrape off or burn off. My buddy Dave had to get a chunk of his ear taken off a couple years back because he never wore a hat. But that's not what this is. This isn't some surface-level rash. It's... the skin itself is just collapsing. It's a structural thing. It's that sunken, rough patch. 

And besides, I don't even know how I'd find the time to go to another doctor. I'm already missing a whole day's pay just being here with you, sitting in this chair, having my eyesight and my sanity questioned, to be honest with you. If I go to a dermatologist, what are they gonna do? Shine a really bright light on my face, poke at it, and charge me another copay just to say, "Yep, that's a sunken patch alright"? I don't need a guy with a medical degree to confirm it's physically present. I have my own two eyes. The rearview mirror in my truck confirms it every single morning at five AM. The mirror in my hallway confirms it. 

So, no, I haven't looked into a second opinion from a skin doctor. I didn't even consider it. I just want someone to help me figure out how to handle this, how to fix how terrible it looks, without me having to run around to a dozen different clinics trying to prove that it's real.
Have you ever had a medical professional physically examine the patch on your face?

Well, no. I mean... examine it how? Like I was just saying about the dermatologist, I haven't gone to anyone specifically for this. And my regular doctor, Dr. Evans? I haven't brought it up to him either. I only see him maybe once a year, if that, for a standard physical. You know, the routine where they check your blood pressure, tell you to lay off the beer and eat less red meat. Last time I was there, he spent fifteen minutes lecturing me about my cholesterol and telling me I need to eat more oatmeal for breakfast. He wasn't looking at the structural integrity of my face. He looked *at* me, sure, but he didn't get up close and inspect my skin or anything like that. 

And honestly, I didn't point it out to him because... well, what's a general practitioner gonna do? Prescribe me some kind of lotion? It's not dry skin. It's not a rash you can just rub some hydrocortisone on and call it a day. It's a physical depression in my face. 

Plus, I just... I don't like going to doctors unless something is actively broken or bleeding. That's just how guys in my trade are. If you can wrap it up or walk it off, you go to work. I missed maybe three days back in 2012 when I threw my lower back out lifting a pallet of cinder blocks the wrong way, and I only went to the clinic then because the site manager forced me to for the workers' comp paperwork. So the idea of making a special appointment, taking more time off work, sitting in a waiting room reading three-year-old magazines just to have a guy poke at my cheek and charge me for the privilege? It just doesn't make any sense to me. 

I don't need a doctor to touch it to prove it's real. I touch it. I feel it every single time I wash my face or shave. I can feel exactly where the skin just dips down. So, no, no medical professional has physically examined it. Just me. And my wife, I guess, when I practically beg her to look at it, but like I said, she just glances at it and tells me I'm crazy.
Have you ever had any injuries or traumatic experiences related to your face?

Injuries? To my face? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, you'd think so, right? Given what I do for a living. I've been on job sites since I was nineteen years old, straight out of high school, and man, the things I've seen out there. You're always dodging stuff—swinging boards, dropped tools, flying gravel when the concrete trucks are pouring. I saw a guy, Mike, back in '98, take the kickback from a power saw right to the jaw. Nasty, nasty stuff. Took about forty stitches and he still has this wicked scar pulling his lip down. You wear your hard hat and your safety glasses, sure, but the rest of your face is just out there exposed to whatever happens. 

But me? I've been lucky, I guess, at least when it comes to taking a hit above the neck. I've smashed my fingers with a hammer more times than I can count, and I already told you about throwing my lower back out a few years ago, but my face has always been completely fine. Never been hit, never been cut open, never been in a car wreck where my head hit the steering wheel or the dash, nothing like that. Not even a broken nose from a bar fight when I was younger and a lot dumber. 

And see, Doc, that's exactly what drives me so crazy about this whole thing! If I had taken a stray piece of scaffolding to the cheek, or if I had fallen and scraped my face up against some rough concrete, then yeah, I’d understand why the skin is collapsing right there. I’d look in the mirror and say, 'Well, that’s from the accident.' It would make sense. There would be a logical reason for it. But there is no reason. Nothing hit me. Nothing happened to me. It's just... deteriorating on its own. It's just sinking in for absolutely no reason at all. So no, no trauma, no injuries. Just this messed up patch that came out of nowhere.
Have you ever thought that your concern about the patch on your face might be related to how you're feeling about yourself, rather than just how you look?

How I'm feeling about myself? I... well, no. I don't really get what you're driving at there, Doc. Like, my self-esteem or something? No, I haven't thought that at all, because it just doesn't make any sense to me. 

I mean, I feel fine about myself as a person. I'm fifty-two years old, I've got a solid union job, I pay my mortgage on time every month, and my kids are grown and doing alright for themselves. I'm a provider. I work hard. I don't sit around naval-gazing or reading self-help books, you know? That's just not who I am or how I was raised. I've never been the type to get all wrapped up in my own head about my feelings. Out on the site, the guys on the crew, we bust each other's chops all day long. If you show up wearing a new shirt or you get a bad haircut, you're gonna hear about it from five different guys for eight hours straight. You gotta have thick skin in my line of work, or you're just not gonna make it. So it's not like I'm some overly sensitive guy who's down in the dumps about who I am. 

My concern about the patch is exactly what it sounds like—it's about the patch. It's about waking up, looking in the bathroom mirror, and seeing this... this cave-in on my cheek that shouldn't be there. It's purely physical. It's not some kind of metaphor for my life. If my truck gets a flat tire on the way to work, I don't sit on the side of the highway wondering if my concern about the tire is actually just me feeling bad about myself. I just see a flat tire that needs fixing. 

That's exactly how I look at this thing on my face. If I had a broken arm, you wouldn't ask me if my concern about the bone sticking out was related to my feelings, right? You'd say, 'Wow, your arm is broken, let's get a cast on that.' I just want to look normal again. I want to be able to go to the hardware store or stand in line at the bank without feeling like everyone is zeroing in on this structural defect on my face. It has absolutely nothing to do with my feelings or my self-worth or whatever else. It's just the physical reality of my skin sinking in, and I just want to know how to fix it.
Have you experienced any major life changes or significant stress in the past year?

Major life changes? Stress? No, no, nothing like that. I mean... my life is about as routine as it gets, Doc. You could set your watch by it. I wake up at 4:30 every single morning, pour my coffee into the same thermos I've had since 2006, and I'm out the door by 5:15 to beat the traffic on the interstate. It's the exact same routine I've had for decades. 

The job sites change, sure. Like, last year we were doing the concrete work for that new commercial park over on Route 9, and right now we're framing up a residential subdivision out past the county line, but it's all the same dirt, the same materials, the same guys on the crew. So work isn't stressing me out any more than it usually does. I mean, yeah, sometimes a lumber delivery is late or the site manager gets on a tear about being behind schedule because of the rain, but that's just the job. That's everyday stuff. You leave that in the truck when you pull into the driveway at the end of the day. 

And at home? Everything's completely quiet. Like I said before, the kids are grown and out of the house. My oldest, Tommy, he's down in Florida doing HVAC, making really good money, and my daughter just had her second baby, so she's busy with her own life. So it's just me and my wife. We paid off the mortgage three years ago, thank god, so we don't even have the bank breathing down our necks anymore. We just eat dinner, watch Jeopardy or maybe a ballgame, and go to sleep. There's no drama. No big moves, no financial ruin, nobody passed away... knock on wood. 

So, no. No big life changes, no hidden stress. I mean, besides this. This is the stress! This patch right here on my cheek, that's the only thing that's changed in my life. If it wasn't for this... this crater sinking into my face, I'd be perfectly fine. That's what I'm trying to get across here. It's not some stress thing making me imagine it. Everything else in my life is completely steady, completely normal. It's just my face that's falling apart.
Has a doctor or nurse ever physically examined the patch on your face?

Yeah, I actually brought it up to my regular guy, Dr. Evans, a couple of months ago when I went in for my annual physical. I made him get right up close to me, right under those bright, harsh fluorescent lights they have in the exam rooms. I even pulled out my phone and showed him these pictures I took sitting in the cab of my truck, because the morning sun comes right through the driver's side window and casts a shadow that really highlights how deep the cave-in is. 

I tried to explain it to him, which is exactly why I'm here talking to you now, because I just can’t stop seeing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. It’s all I look at. Whether it's in photos my wife takes with the grandkids or just me staring in the bathroom mirror while I'm shaving, it is just glaring right back at me. It makes that whole side of me look completely old and just... beat-up. Like I'm lopsided and deteriorating. 

But you know what Evans did? He shined his little penlight on my cheek, rubbed his thumb over the spot for maybe two seconds, and then stepped back and told me he didn't see anything to worry about. Said it was just "normal aging." Normal aging! I couldn't believe it. It’s like I’m taking crazy pills, Doc, because people keep saying they barely notice anything. My wife says it, the guys at work say it, and then a medical doctor says it. They just glance at it and brush it off like it's nothing. But how can they not see it? How can a trained doctor look right at this rough, sunken-in crater and tell me it's barely noticeable? That's why I can't just let it go, because I know what I'm looking at, and I know it's not normal.
Do you think your perception of the patch on your face is affecting how you see your body as a whole?

My body as a whole? I... no, I don't really follow you there, Doc. Like, do I think my whole body is falling apart because of this spot on my cheek? No, absolutely not. 

Look at me, I've been doing heavy physical labor for over thirty years. Framing, pouring concrete, hauling lumber, you name it. My body is a machine. Sure, my knees ache a little when a cold front moves in, and I've got a twinge in my lower back if I lift a bag of cement the wrong way, but that's just miles on the odometer, you know? I'm fifty-two, I expect a little wear and tear on the chassis. I don't look in the mirror and hate my chest or my arms or my legs. I can still out-work half the twenty-somethings that show up on the job site with their brand-new boots and zero work ethic. My body does exactly what I need it to do. It puts food on the table. So, no, I don't have any issues with my body as a whole. I'm perfectly fine with the rest of me. 

The problem is just... this. It's entirely localized. It's right here on my cheek. It's not spreading to my arms or making me think I'm out of shape or something. It's just this one specific, sunken-in, rough crater on my face. 

It's kind of like... well, think about it like a classic car, right? Say you've got this great old muscle car. The engine purrs, the transmission is smooth, the interior is mint, but there's this massive, ugly, caved-in dent right on the front fender. You don't look at the dent and think the whole car is garbage. You know the car runs great. But you also can't stop staring at the dent because it just completely ruins the front end. It's all you can see when you look at it. That's exactly what this is. My body is fine. It's just this one glaring defect on my face that I can't stand, and if somebody could just tell me how to patch it up, I'd be a hundred percent again.
Do you think you would be satisfied with your appearance if the patch on your face were to suddenly disappear?

Would I be satisfied? Man, I... I don't even know how to answer that, Doc. I really don't. I mean, you say "suddenly disappear" like someone's just gonna wave a magic wand over my cheek and poof, the dent is gone and the fender is brand new again. I can't even picture that anymore. I really can't. 

Because every single morning, like I was telling you, I'm up at 4:30, I go into the bathroom to splash some cold water on my face and wake myself up, and boom, there it is. It's the very first thing I see. It's like my eyes are just drawn straight to that rough, caved-in spot before I even register the rest of my face. I've spent so many hours just staring at it, tilting my head this way and that way, trying to see how the bathroom light catches the edges of it. 

So if it just vanished... I don't know. I'd like to sit here and tell you, "Oh yeah, absolutely, I'd be a hundred percent happy, case closed, I'd never worry about a mirror again." But honestly? I'm not sure. Because it’s been taking up so much space in my head for so long now. When I'm on the site, tying rebar or whatever, and one of the guys comes over to hand me a tool, half the time I'm thinking, "Is he staring at the crater? Is he looking at that shadow on my cheek?" If the patch was just gone tomorrow... would I still think people were staring? Would I just be waiting for it to come back? Would I start noticing something else? 

I mean, I'm not a vain guy. I'm not trying to be a male model here. I don't need to look twenty-five again.
